title: Maharashtra Bans Analogue Paneer for One Year, Violators Face Jail Time
excerpt: The state escalates from mandatory disclosure to an outright prohibition on fake paneer in all hotels and restaurants, with penalties including six months imprisonment.
body:
• Maharashtra has imposed a one-year ban on the use of analogue paneer in all hotels, restaurants and food outlets, escalating from mandatory disclosure rules introduced in May 2026.
  • Violators face up to six months in jail and a fine of Rs 1 lakh under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
  • The state's FDA inspected nearly 1,500 establishments during its initial crackdown in May, uncovering widespread use of non-dairy substitutes sold as real paneer.
  • FSSAI is studying Maharashtra's approach as a potential model for a national ban on analogue paneer.

Maharashtra has banned the use of analogue paneer in all hotels, restaurants and food-service establishments across the state for one year, marking India's most aggressive action yet against the sale of non-dairy substitutes passed off as genuine cottage cheese.

The order, issued by the state's Food and Drug Administration, imposes criminal penalties on violators: up to six months of imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh. It applies to hotels, restaurants, caterers, street food vendors and packaged food suppliers operating anywhere in Maharashtra.

From Disclosure to an Outright Ban

The ban represents a significant escalation. In April 2026, the FDA had ordered all food businesses to disclose the use of cheese analogues on menu cards, bills and display boards, with enforcement beginning May 1. FDA Minister Narhari Zirwal and Commissioner Sridhar Dube Patil led the initial crackdown, during which 1,496 establishments were inspected in the first 10 days alone.

But officials found that disclosure alone was insufficient. Multiple complaints continued to pour in about restaurants serving analogue paneer without adequate labelling, prompting the state to move from transparency requirements to a complete prohibition.

"Licences of traders and vendors involved in such fraudulent practices will be cancelled immediately."

— Narhari Zirwal, FDA Minister, Maharashtra

What Is Analogue Paneer?

Real paneer is made entirely from milk. Analogue paneer, by contrast, is manufactured using vegetable oils — typically palm oil — along with starch, emulsifiers and sometimes milk solids. It is engineered to mimic the appearance, texture and cooking properties of dairy paneer, making it nearly impossible for consumers to distinguish once it is part of a prepared dish.

The cost difference is substantial. Analogue paneer can be produced at a fraction of the price of genuine dairy paneer, giving unscrupulous operators a financial incentive to substitute it without informing customers. Under Section 18(2)(e) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, consumers have the right to know the ingredients of the food they purchase.

How to Spot the Difference

The FDA has recommended several methods for consumers to identify fake paneer. Genuine paneer has a slightly grainy texture and a fresh, milky smell. When heated, real paneer softens but retains its shape, while analogue paneer tends to become rubbery or excessively stretchy. A simple home test involves rubbing a piece between your fingers — real paneer crumbles, while the analogue version feels slick due to its oil content.

FSSAI relies on two scientific markers for laboratory detection: fatty acid profiling and the beta-sitosterol test. Beta-sitosterol, a plant sterol found in vegetable oils, is virtually absent in pure milk fat. The regulator has set a threshold of 7 parts per million; anything above that confirms adulteration with vegetable oil.

National Implications

Maharashtra's initiative has drawn the attention of the central government's Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. FSSAI is reportedly studying the state's approach as a potential template for a nationwide ban on analogue paneer, according to government officials familiar with the deliberations.

India is the world's largest producer of milk, yet the widespread use of cheap dairy substitutes in the food-service industry has long been an open secret. The Indian Dairy Association has consistently advocated for stricter standards, arguing that analogue products undermine both consumer trust and the livelihoods of millions of dairy farmers.

What's Next

The one-year ban gives Maharashtra time to assess the impact of a complete prohibition before deciding on a permanent policy. The Hotel and Restaurant Association (Western India) has backed the initiative and is collaborating with the FDA on compliance training for its members. Consumers dining out in Maharashtra can now report suspected violations through the FDA's complaint portal, with authorities pledging swift action against offenders.
nri_angle: NRI visitors and the diaspora frequently consume paneer dishes when traveling to India; the ban ensures they receive genuine dairy products at restaurants.
